Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Rivera (BrightCart Lead Eng), Luis Ortega (BrightCart CTO), Priya Singh (BrightCart Platform Eng)

Redwood does a focused SDK walkthrough for Python and TypeScript quickstarts, covers auth (API keys, service accounts, SSO notes), environment setup, Console overview for routes/keys, and Redwood Optimize suggestions. Customer asks about Dedicated vs Hosted, data residency, and benchmark expectations. Next steps agreed: hand over quickstart repos, trial org, and schedule a POC benchmark run.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna run through a short SDK integration walkthrough today, focus on Python and TypeScript quickstarts, then a few notes on auth and env setup. Samir's gonna demo a live snippet.
[00:18] Maya: Thanks, Jordan. Quick note, we've got about 45 minutes; Luis may need to hop after 35 if we get into deep infra.
[00:26] Jordan: Totally fine. Samir, over to you.
[00:30] Samir: Cool, thanks. So first slide, sorry slide deck is linked in the chat, but I'm gonna start with the Python quickstart. We have a pip package redwood-inference, you can install via pip install redwood-inference, or for JS there's @redwood/inference on npm.
[00:48] Priya: Is the package name exactly that? We had a previous note where the name was redwood-sdk in our notes, just want to confirm.
[00:55] Samir: Good call, it's a little confusing, the official pip package is redwood_inference (underscore) but the NPM package is @redwood/inference, docs show both, I'll send the link. Sometimes the auto transcript spoils the underscore as a dash, apologies.
[01:12] Jordan: We'll put canonical repo links in the follow-up. For auth, the simplest path is API keys for dev and trial. For production we recommend service accounts + short-lived tokens or SSO for interactive users.
[01:26] Luis: On data retention and encryption — we need to know if logs can be disabled and how keys are managed. We use KMS in GCP.
[01:34] Samir: Yep. For Hosted API you can opt out of retention, and we support customer-managed keys via KMS or HSM in Private deployments. For Dedicated there's also an option to bring your own KMS; I'll share the security docs.
[01:48] Maya: Great. Walk us through env setup — what env vars should we set for local dev, CI, and a service account?
[01:56] Samir: Locally it's simple: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-..., or for service accounts you use REDWOOD_CLIENT_ID and REDWOOD_CLIENT_SECRET to mint tokens via our token endpoint. For Node quickstarts we show dotenv usage, and for Python we demonstrate using os.environ or a secrets manager in CI.
[02:15] Priya: Do you support gcloud/gs-releated metadata credentials?
[02:18] Samir: We have integrations documented for GCP service accounts and AWS IAM role chaining for Private & Dedicated. Hosted supports static keys but for long term we recommend swapping to federation or KMS-backed service tokens.
[02:29] Jordan: Ok now Samir will run a short code demo — no sound heavy benchmark yet, just end-to-end request to the API. Samir?
[02:36] Samir: I'll share my screen. First the Python example: from redwood_inference import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.text.generate(model='redwood-1-small', prompt='Summarize: our checkout flow...') — response streaming is supported via client.stream... You can choose sync or streaming depending on the SDK.
[02:58] Maya: Are there typed response objects? We want strong typing in our services.
[03:03] Samir: Yes Python objects have attributes but for TypeScript the SDK returns strongly typed interfaces — e.g., GenerateResponse with tokens, usage, and metadata. Small caveat, sometimes the field names in older SDKs had slightly different names, but docs show latest.
[03:20] Priya: Any examples for tool calling / function call style outputs?
[03:23] Samir: Yep, we demo function calling: you define a schema for the function, the model can return a structured output matching that schema and the SDK will deserialize it. We have an example where the model returns JSON for an order object and we directly hydrate our types.
[03:37] Jordan: Quick note — Optimize integrations: batching and prefix caching can be toggled from the SDK or console. For high-throughput routes, we recommend using the SDK batching helper so you don't have to manage manual queues.
[03:48] Luis: How does batching impact latency? We're sensitive to p95 latency for checkout flows.
[03:53] Samir: There's a tradeoff. Batching improves throughput and cost but can increase tail latency if you wait for batch fill. Redwood has adaptive batching: it will guarantee a latency SLO and dynamically batch within that window. For checkout we often recommend smaller batch sizes and aggressive timeouts to keep p95 in check. We'll share recommended config values per workload.
[04:11] Maya: And quantization / model variants — if we pick a cheaper quantized variant, what's the expected perf delta?
[04:17] Samir: Typical ballparks: 4-bit quantized can save 2-4x cost with small throughput and slightly higher latency in some configs; depends on model family. We'll run a quick benchmark during the POC to give you exact numbers for your prompt shapes.
[04:32] [05:00] Jordan: Switching to the Console quick tour — Samir, can you show API keys, routes, and logs?
[05:06] Samir: Sure. Console lets you create routes that map to model + config, attach API keys, set quotas, and enable autoscaling for dedicated pools. Logs show per-request latency, token counts, and an errors tab. Note: sometimes the console labels differ a bit in older screenshots, but live UI is accurate.
[05:28] Priya: Do logs include full prompt text? We need to mask or avoid storing PII.
[05:33] Samir: You can opt out of storing prompts; there's a toggle per-route to disable prompt retention. Also we redact based on patterns, and for Private deployments you can configure retention and disable logs entirely.
[05:44] Maya: For CI/CD, what's the recommended approach to rotate keys?
[05:47] Jordan: Use short-lived tokens from a service account, rotate via your secrets manager; we have a sample GitHub Actions snippet in the quickstart repo.
[05:58] Samir: I'm pasting the quickstart repo link in chat: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts (note: link in transcript may be slightly off, follow-up will include canonical links).
[06:10] Luis: For the POC, we plan to test two flows: checkout personalization (real-time) and batch embeddings for retraining recommendations. Any special guidance?
[06:20] Samir: For real-time checkout keep routes with low-latency SLOs, avoid large context windows, use prefix caching for repeated templates. For batch embeddings use our batch endpoints or the embeddings streaming to S3. We have an Optimize rule set for embeddings that recommends quantization and throughput-backed Dedicated pools.
[06:38] Maya: Can we run a small synthetic benchmark ourselves or do you run it?
[06:42] Jordan: We can hand off a bench harness — Samir will run a Redwood-run with your sample prompt and return numbers. Also, we can give you a script to run locally so you can reproduce.
[06:52] Samir: I'll add a runnable bench tool to the repo. It uses our SDK to hit the route with a configurable concurrency and records latency and token usage. I'll also include sample Postman/HTTP examples for quick smoke tests.
[07:05] Priya: Regarding Private deployment — how different is the SDK usage?
[07:09] Samir: Same SDK calls but the endpoint changes to your private control plane domain, and auth goes through your SSO or service accounts. All SDK config knobs are identical so you don't change code. That's a big selling point: same interface across Hosted, Dedicated, Private.
[07:23] Maya: Sounds good. A few smaller asks: provide a sample env file, a sample GitHub Actions snippet, and a short runbook for key rotation and incident playbook.
[07:32] Jordan: We'll include those in the follow-up.
[07:35] [08:00] Jordan: Any blockers on procurement or security that would stop a quick POC?
[08:06] Luis: We need SOC2 docs, KMS integration details, and a standard NDA review for any data we might send. Also internal legal wants to confirm data residency for EU traffic.
[08:17] Samir: We'll attach SOC2, and our Private/Dedicated options support EU regions and customer-managed keys. I'll have the security packet in the follow-up.
[08:27] Maya: Cool. On success criteria for the POC: 1) p95 latency under 200ms for 1k qps simulated in our checkout microservice; 2) cost per 1k requests under $X (we'll provide the X); 3) embedding recall within 3% of current baseline.
[08:44] Jordan: Great, concrete goals. We'll scope the bench around those.
[08:50] [09:15] Samir: Quick demo wrap — here's a TypeScript example pasted in chat (also in repo): import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const res = await client.chat.create({ model: 'redwood-1-chat', messages: [...] }); console.log(res.choices[0].message.content);
[09:35] Maya: Any gotchas for serverless environments like Vercel or Cloud Run?
[09:39] Samir: Cold start + KV cache: we recommend warming and using client-side caching; adjust batch helper for serverless since processes are ephemeral. For Cloud Run use a warmup probe and reuse a client singleton.
[09:53] Priya: For Node, how heavy is the dependency? Any native bindings?
[09:57] Samir: Pure JS, no native bindings. Python is pure wheel with optional C-extensions for faster streaming in certain environments. Docs note the optional extras.
[10:09] Luis: About pricing — can you provide estimate for our expected QPS?
[10:13] Jordan: We'll share an estimate after you provide sample workload and expected token counts. Pricing will include hosted per-token and a Dedicated reserved capacity option if you'd like predictable unit costs.
[10:23] Jordan: Okay last section — rollout and SDK versioning. We support pinning model versions in routes so you can canary and do A/B tests via the Console.
[10:33] Samir: Also the SDK includes a local validation tool to simulate request shape against the route config so you can detect mismatches before deploy.
[10:40] Maya: That would help.
[10:44] Jordan: Alright let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[10:47] Jordan: Recap: we showed Python & TS quickstarts, env/auth patterns, Console features, Optimize recommendations (batching/caching/quantization), and agreed POC success criteria. Action items and links will be sent.
[10:58] Luis: Thanks folks, appreciate the clarity. We'll aim to share sample prompts and the cost target by Tuesday.
[11:04] Maya: We may want a short SE-led bench run next Thursday — can you two be available?
[11:09] Jordan: Yep, we'll propose times after we send the trial org.
[11:13] Samir: I'll follow up with the repo, security packet, and bench harness.
[11:18] Jordan: Thanks everyone. End call.
